Route 101 Pilot Data & Incident Analysis 
Route 101 Overview 
- 14.2 km corridor connecting the northern districts to downtown 
- 12 smart stations with real-time arrival info and, at 4 stops, charging heads 
- Dispatched from the Metro Terminal Hub, led by Operations Supervisor Marcus Vance 
Incident Case Study — July 12 Pilot Run 
During a regional heatwave, VoltBus Unit #09 triggered a Level 1 Thermal Warning while stopped at Stop 7 (Oak 
Street). 
Detail 
Value 
Vehicle 
VoltBus Unit #09 
Location 
Stop 7 — Oak Street 
Conditions 
39°C, direct sun, heatwave 
Cause 
Two back-to-back 450 kW rapid charges in 45 minutes 
Alert Level 
Level 1 — Warning 
How It Was Resolved 
- Cooling pumps automatically ramped to 100%, as designed 
- Charging speed was reduced until the battery cooled down 
- Unit #09 stayed in service throughout — no passengers were affected and the route stayed on schedule 
- Temperature normalized in 14 minutes, well before it could escalate to a Level 2 Emergency 
Follow-Up Action 
Engineering, under Elena Rostova, issued a new rule: during heatwaves above 35°C, Stop 7 allows only one rapid 
charge per layover instead of two. Since this change, no further thermal warnings have occurred on Route 101.

Executive Summary & Program Objectives 
Program Overview 
VoltBus is MMIG's flagship autonomous electric bus program, built to prove that a fully electric, self-driving 
transit fleet can run safely and reliably on real city streets. 
The program is led by Chief Systems Architect Elena Rostova, whose team owns final sign-off on every safety 
and engineering decision before a change reaches passenger service. 
- Electric propulsion — zero tailpipe emissions on every route 
- Autonomous driving — supported by redundant sensors and a dedicated safety system 
- Smart stations — real-time passenger info and charging integration 
Program Objectives 
- Prove reliable, all-electric transit service on a busy urban corridor 
- Validate the onboard safety system under real traffic and pedestrian conditions 
- Build a repeatable depot maintenance model ready for fleet-wide scale-up 
- Collect the safety data needed for full autonomy certification 
Key System Milestones 
Phase 
Status 
What It Covers 
Phase I — Platform Validation 
Complete 
Chassis and battery certification, closed-course 
autonomy testing, depot setup 
Phase II — Controlled Pilot 
Active 
Live service on Route 101 with a safety operator 
onboard at all times 
Phase III — Network Expansion 
Planned 
Rollout to five more corridors and removal of the 
onboard safety operator 
 
Where We Are Today 
The program is currently in Phase II. To move into Phase III, VoltBus needs 90 straight days of stable 
performance on Route 101 with zero unresolved safety incidents.

[00:00 - 00:04] Good morning, everyone. This is Elena Rostova, Chief Systems Architect.
[00:04 - 00:13] Today is August 21st, 2026, and we are kicking off our monthly engineering review for phase two operations on Route 101.
[00:13 - 00:20] On the line, we have Marcus Vance from Operations at the Metro Terminal Hub and David Miller, lead technician down at Depot Gamma.
[00:20 - 00:24] Marcus, let's start with high-level throughput.
[00:24 - 00:29] Thanks, Elena. Route 101 has had a solid month overall.
[00:29 - 00:34] We cleared approximately 48,000 passenger rides across our 12 smart stations.
[00:34 - 00:41] The 14.2 km corridor is holding an average end-to-end travel time of about 24 minutes.
[00:41 - 00:52] Over at the Metro Terminal Hub, our 450 kilowatt-pantograph charger is averaging 6 to 8 minutes per rapid top-up, keeping our turnaround times tight.
[00:52 - 00:54] That's great, Marcus.
[00:54 - 00:58] Now, let's dig into the primary incident from last month's log.
[00:58 - 01:03] The thermal event on July 12 involving Vultbus Unit No. 09.
[01:03 - 01:07] Marcus set the scene for us regarding environmental conditions.
[01:07 - 01:11] Right. It was a severe regional heat wave.
[01:11 - 01:17] Ambient ground temp reached 39 degrees Celsius at Stop 7, Oak Street.
[01:17 - 01:26] Unit No. 09 had just logged back to back 450 kilowatt rapid charges at the Metro Terminal Hub within a 45-minute window
[01:26 - 01:29] to keep up with peak holiday traffic.
[01:29 - 01:37] As it arrived at Stop 7, the internal sensor suite flagged an LFP2 battery-packed temperature crossing 48 degrees Celsius.
[01:37 - 01:43] Which triggered a level 1 warning state in perception OS version 4.2.

updates 
Any bus that trips a Level 2 thermal event is automatically routed to Depot-Gamma for inspection before it can 
return to service. 
Maintenance SOP — Battery Cell Imbalance 
Lead Technician David Miller maintains the standard procedure for handling battery cell imbalances at Depot-
Gamma. If a battery pack shows more than 5% internal resistance imbalance between cell groups, it's 
automatically flagged for inspection. 
- Step 1 — Isolate: the affected battery pack is disconnected and put into diagnostic mode 
- Step 2 — Run DR-88: Diagnostic Routine 88 tests each cell group's resistance and capacity against its 
original baseline 
- Step 3 — Classify: the pack is marked as fine, degraded (replace within 30 days), or faulty (replace 
immediately) 
- Step 4 — Sign off: results are logged and countersigned by Technician Miller before the bus returns to 
Marcus Vance's dispatch pool 
 
No Shortcuts 
A bus can never return to service after a DR-88 check without a documented pass — no exceptions, even 
under schedule pressure. 
What's Next 
- Depot-Beta (East District): new facility in progress ahead of Phase III 
- Two additional 450 kW charging heads planned for the Metro Terminal Hub 
- Ongoing grid capacity review with the Regional Utilities Commission
